Attribute coverage counts each attribute on its own: three lanes and 60 km/h can both be covered by runs that never drove 60 km/h on a three-lane road. A module already says such a combination, so a module can be covered as a situation:

OddModule(
    "three_lane_cruise",
    include_and=[lanes.equals(3), speed.between(55, 65)],
    situation=True,
    cover_by="meters", target=200, min_stay=3.0,   # 200 m, counting stays of 3 s or more
)

Every tick, the module's verdict (which the ODD works out anyway) is a sample of the item odd.situation.three_lane_cruise, which has one bucket, holds. A tick where the module holds is a sample in it. A tick where it fails, or is inactive, ends the stay. A tick where it rests on missing values ends the stay too, and is counted apart as unknown. target, cover_by and min_stay work as for attributes (docs/coverage.md). The report lists situations in a group of their own, Situation coverage.

A situation is what the runs should drive, not a bound of the ODD: with roots left out, a situation nothing refers to is not a root candidate. To make it a bound too, refer to it from a root, or name it in roots.

docs.title: Built-in probes
docs.text:
These live in autoware_carla_scenario.odd:

Probe Returns Read from ego_speed_kph float, km/h Ego velocity speed_limit_kph float, km/h Lanelet2 speed_limit tag, else CARLA lanelet_speed_limit_kph float, km/h Lanelet2 speed_limit tag lanelet_location str Lanelet2 location tag (urban, nonurban, ...) lanelet_subtype str Lanelet2 subtype tag (road, highway, ...) in_junction bool CARLA waypoint lane_count int Driving lanes in the ego's direction (CARLA, outside junctions) illumination ILLUMINATION_LEVELS Sun altitude rain, fog INTENSITY_LEVELS CARLA weather (0-100) visibility float, m How far drivers see, as the run's weather left it (Visibility follows the weather); nothing when the run set none traffic_density TRAFFIC_DENSITY_LEVELS Other vehicles within NEARBY_RADIUS_M pedestrian_nearby bool A walker within NEARBY_RADIUS_M The Lanelet2 probes need the run to have a Lanelet2 map (map.lanelet2_path). Without one they return nothing.

The probes whose value the map alone decides (speed_limit_kph, lanelet_speed_limit_kph, lanelet_location, lanelet_subtype, in_junction, lane_count) can also read it off a lanelet, which is how a planned route is checked before a run (Checking a planned route) and how a sweep picks the road a drawn case is on (The road a case is on).

What they read off a lanelet is public too, for code that has to judge a lanelet exactly as the ODD does: lanelet_in_junction(lanelet) (a turn_direction tag, scenery.junction), lanelet_road_type(lanelet) (the subtype tag, scenery.road_type) and lanelet_speed_limit(lanelet) (the speed_limit tag, km/h). The adversities' location gate reads them (autoware_carla_scenario.adversity.location).

Import them from autoware_carla_scenario.odd itself (from autoware_carla_scenario.odd import rain). The Codon model that checks an ODD has no probes submodule.

docs.title: Scenario measures
docs.text:
The road users a scenario stages -- a vehicle ahead in the next lane, a pedestrian running out -- are not read by ODD probes: they are measures of the scenario, under keys the framework fixes (autoware_carla_scenario.measures). Every BaseScenario has these, read generically around the ego:

Key Unit Version Reads vehicle_ahead_gap_m m 2 The free road to the nearest vehicle ahead on the ego's lane or a lane beside it: its rear bumper less the ego's front bumper, along the ego's lane on the Lanelet2 map (up to AHEAD_RANGE_M); a vehicle about to cut in is measured from before it changes lanes vehicle_ahead_relative_speed_kph km/h 2 That vehicle's speed along the ego's lane less the ego's crossing_pedestrian_gap_m m How far ahead the nearest pedestrian ahead that is moving was when it set off, held while it crosses crossing_pedestrian_speed_ms m/s That pedestrian's speed stop_line_distance_m m 1 Along the ego's lane, from its front bumper to the nearest stop line ahead -- a traffic light's, a traffic sign's or a road marking's, as a stop_line_offset binding finds them -- up to AHEAD_RANGE_M, on any branch of the lane where it forks (the measure does not know the route); nothing without a lane to read along

The pedestrian measures read in the ego's frame: ahead along its heading, within PEDESTRIAN_LATERAL_M of its centre line.

docs.title: The vehicle ahead
docs.text:
The vehicle-ahead measures read along the road, as a driver would say "the car in front is 15 m ahead", and from the map:

  • The ego's lane is the lanelet the ego is on -- of those under its origin (within ON_LANELET_M), the one whose centreline runs closest to its heading, within EGO_LANE_HEADING_DEG -- with every lanelet following it up to AHEAD_RANGE_M ahead and the lanelets behind it. Where the lane branches, every branch is the ego's lane: the measure does not know the route, so a vehicle ahead on either branch counts. Behind, the lane runs back one way only, through the first of the lanelets before each (Lanelet2's previous(...)[0]), where lanes merge; a lanelet joining the ego's lane is not its lane, nor beside it. Its arc length s runs along their centrelines, on from one to the next.
  • A vehicle counts when its origin is on one of those lanelets, or on a lanelet beside one of them -- its left or right neighbour in the Lanelet2 routing graph, whether a lane change is allowed across the line or not -- and further along the ego's lane than the ego's origin. A lane two over, an oncoming lane or a vehicle off the lanelets does not count, however near.
  • The gap is s of the vehicle's rear bumper less s of the ego's front bumper. A bumper is the middle of the end of the actor's bounding box, along its own heading (Bumpers, bumpers_of), and it is projected onto the ego's lane: onto the lanelet the vehicle is on, or the one it is beside, and those before and after it. So the gap does not depend on where the lanelets beside each other are cut or how long they are -- the outer lane of a bend is longer than the inner one, and the same s on the two is not side by side -- and on a bend it is the distance along the road, not a straight line. A vehicle on the ego's own lane that overlaps it reads a negative gap; one in a lane beside that overlaps it (its rear bumper behind the ego's front bumper) is alongside, not ahead, and does not count, so it never hides the vehicle that is ahead. One beside and ahead of the ego counts, which is how a vehicle about to cut in is measured before it changes lanes.
  • The relative speed is the vehicle's velocity along the lane's tangent at its rear bumper less the ego's along the tangent at its front bumper: two vehicles keeping pace round a bend read 0 though their headings differ.

Without a lane to measure along -- no Lanelet2 map loaded, or the ego on no lanelet that runs its way -- the measures fall back to the geometric definition: a vehicle ahead of the ego's origin within three LANE_HALF_WIDTH_M of its centre line counts, and the gap is bumper to bumper along the ego's heading. The run logs a warning the first time, and the coverage file says how many frames each definition read (measures.vehicle_ahead_gap_m.definitions: along_lane, geometric; vehicle_ahead_definitions() in Python). The geometric definition, too, does not count a vehicle alongside in the next lane.

A reading costs about 3 ms with ten vehicles around the ego on CARLA Town04_Opt (it was some 170 ms). The ego's lane is found once and kept while its lanelet is still the ego's -- the ego on it, running its way, and no lanelet overlapping it (found by geometry, however the map cuts a fork's branches or an exit into lanelets) running closer to the ego's heading -- and the whole map is searched only when it is not (or, off the lanelets, once the ego has moved 2 m or turned 5°); a vehicle is placed by the lane's own lanelets, not by searching the map; and a projection reads only the stretch of a centreline near the point. The Lanelet2 routing graph the lane is read from -- some 25 s to build on Town04_Opt -- is built in the run's setup whenever the ODD maps a vehicle-ahead measure that the scenario reads with the built-in one -- not for one it replaced with register_measure (prepare_measures) -- with every lanelet's bounding box, not on the first tick. A failed reading reads nothing and is warned of once a run.

docs.title: Measure versions
docs.text:
A measure's version (Measure.version, measure_version(key)) says which definition it reads with, and is raised whenever what it reads changes meaning. The vehicle-ahead measures are version 2. Version 1 (before autoware-carla-scenario 12.0) read the gap centre to centre along the ego's heading -- 4.75 m more than version 2 for a Lincoln MKZ behind a Mini on CARLA 0.10 -- and counted a vehicle within three half-lanes of the ego's centre line, whatever the map.

Coverage keeps the versions apart. openodd's merge treats two coverage items as the same when their name, buckets, event and criteria agree; it does not read their description. So the cover item of an ODD attribute mapped onto a measure past version 1 is written under its version, odd.dynamic.vehicle_ahead_gap@v2: merged with files written before, the report lists odd.dynamic.vehicle_ahead_gap (version 1) and odd.dynamic.vehicle_ahead_gap@v2 (version 2) apart, never one bucket's hits added to the other's. The mark is @v<n>, not #<n>: #<n> is the suffix openodd's merge gives an item it meets defined differently (version 1 files whose buckets changed merge as odd.dynamic.vehicle_ahead_gap#2), and openodd's sampler adds up an item's #<n> definitions. A coverage-driven sweep (strategy: coverage) reads only the current version: OddSampler hands openodd's sampler the @v2 items under the attribute's own item name and leaves the older ones out (current_measure_coverage), so a coverage_from that also holds version 1's files is safe. The 12.0.0 release wrote version 2 as #2; those files read as version 1, and their hits are left out of a coverage-driven sweep on purpose: since 12.0.0 a vehicle alongside in the next lane no longer counts as ahead, which changed what version 2 reads, not only its name. Each coverage file also lists the measures its ODD reads under measures, with their version, unit and text. A scenario that replaces a built-in measure (register_measure) promises the same quantity, so its replacement carries the built-in's version.

Each reads nothing (missing) while there is no such road user. A scenario that knows better replaces one -- it knows which actor is its cut-in vehicle -- or adds one of its own:

class MyCutIn(BaseScenario):
    def setup(self) -> None:
        ...
        self.register_measure(VEHICLE_AHEAD_GAP_M, self._gap_to_my_npc)

An ODD maps its taxonomy onto measures: in Python with scenario_measure(key) as the attribute's probe, in a binding file with measure: in place of probe::

OddAttribute(
    "dynamic.vehicle_ahead_gap",
    scenario_measure(VEHICLE_AHEAD_GAP_M),
    unit="m",
    buckets=[0, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100],
)

probes:
  headway: {measure: vehicle_ahead_gap_m, buckets: [0, 10, 20, 30]}

The attribute then reads the running scenario's measure, its replacement included, in the measure's unit: an attribute mapped onto a built-in measure takes its unit, and one given that is not it is refused. The keys are in the Codon model (from autoware_carla_scenario.measures import VEHICLE_AHEAD_GAP_M), so a scenario or a Python ODD naming them is checked like any other (Static Check): autoware_carla_scenario.measures is modelled whole, Measure, BUILT_IN_MEASURES, read_measure(), check_measure_key() and measured_scenario() included. A Measure is frozen, as a Metric is: assigning to one of its fields fails the check, as it fails the run. A scenario may build its own (Measure("my_measure", read, "m")); the check calls its read with a world and refuses one that returns anything but a float or an Optional[float]. A metric's keys are modelled the same way (Metrics): autoware_carla_scenario.metrics is modelled whole, Metric and BUILT_IN_METRICS included. The ODD names a measure key, never a scenario; the scenario names its measures, never the ODD. The default ODD maps dynamic.vehicle_ahead_gap, dynamic.vehicle_ahead_relative_speed, dynamic.crossing_pedestrian_gap and dynamic.crossing_pedestrian_speed onto the four built-in measures; the two of the vehicle ahead count stays of 1 s or more (min_stay), so a gap the ego only closes through is not covered.

docs.title: Measures and metrics
docs.text: A measure reads a condition the ego drives in: what the scenario sets up. How the ego drives -- whether it collides, leaves the road, drives against the traffic, how close it comes to other road users -- is an outcome, read by a metric (Metrics). An ODD cannot map onto a metric: scenario_measure("offroad"), or measure: offroad in a binding file, is refused. Were it allowed, the ego's own driving would decide whether a run is inside the domain it is tested in, and an ODD excluding offroad would report a run that left the road as outside the ODD rather than as failed. A run watches a metric with MetricCondition instead.

docs.title: Writing an ODD in OpenODD YAML
docs.text:
The OpenODD files are plain OpenODD 1.0. The example below follows the standard's own examples (Code 170, 171 and 192):

# taxonomy.yml
TAXONOMY:
    environment_conditions:
        rainfall_rate: float precipitation_rate
        rainfall_level:                       # literals defined by ranges: ordered
            no_rain:
                rainfall_rate: "< 0.1 mm/h"
            light_rain:
                rainfall_rate: "[0.1 .. 2.5] mm/h"
            heavy_rain:
                rainfall_rate: "> 2.5 mm/h"
        wind_speed: float velocity
    scenery:
        road_type: [road, highway, road_shoulder]
        lane_count: integer count

# odd.yml
IMPORT:
    - taxonomy.yml

ODD:
    odd1:
        TITLE: The baseline ODD
        INCLUDE_AND:
            low_speed_roads: true
            needs_wind: true
        EXCLUDE_OR:
            bad_weather: true

MODULES:
    low_speed_roads:
        INCLUDE_AND:
            road_type: [road]
            lane_count: "< 3"
    bad_weather_1:
        LABEL: bad_weather
        INCLUDE_OR:
            rainfall_level: ">= heavy_rain"
            wind_speed: "> 50 km/h"
    needs_wind:
        EXCLUDE_OR:
            wind_speed: unknown               # the wind speed is required

The binding file is this framework's own. It says which probe measures each concept, and its buckets:

# urban.yaml
openodd: [odd.yml]                 # relative to this file
name: urban                        # default: this file's stem
text: Urban roads, fair weather
probes:
  road_type: {probe: lanelet_subtype}
  rainfall_rate: {probe: my_package.probes:rain_rate_mm_h, unit: mm/h}
  wind_speed: {probe: my_package.probes:wind_mps, unit: m/s}
  lane_count: {probe: lane_count, values: [1, 2, 3, 4], cover_by: meters, target: 200, min_stay: 2}

Run with odd=path/to/urban.yaml. An OpenODD file on its own can be named too, but then nothing is measured: every concept is missing.

docs.title: Taxonomies and modules from git
docs.text:
An openodd entry can name a file in a git repository at a revision, so a taxonomy or a module library kept elsewhere is used as it was at that revision:

# urban.yaml
openodd:
  - git: https://example.com/odd/taxonomy.git
    rev: 'v1.2.0'                  # a tag, a branch, or a commit
    path: taxonomy.yml             # a list for several files
  - git: git@example.com:odd/modules.git
    rev: '3f2a9c1e0b7d4a6c8e5f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d'
    path: odd/urban.yml
  - local_overrides.yml            # relative to this file
probes:
  ...
  • An IMPORT is looked for next to the importing file first, and then in the other sources: the directory of each file named, and the root of each repository. The standard makes file names unique within one transmission, so odd/urban.yml in one repository can IMPORT: [taxonomy.yml] from another. A name found in two sources is refused.
  • git fetch does the fetching, so url is anything it takes, with the credentials it is configured with. Prompts are turned off, and the ext:: transport is refused.
  • Repositories and checkouts are cached in $AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_ODD_CACHE when it is set, else openodd's $OPENODD_CACHE (default ~/.cache/openodd). A full commit id checked out once is read from the cache without the network; a tag or a branch is fetched on every load, to learn which commit it names now. Pin a commit for runs that must be reproducible.
  • Quote rev: unquoted, a commit id of digits and one e (1630255e36) or a long one of digits only is read as a number, and looked for as one (1.630255e+36).
  • Fetching needs git, which the scenario image does not have. A run there can still read a source pinned to a full commit id, from a cache filled beforehand (scenario-odd show urban.yaml with the same cache directory) and mounted at $AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_ODD_CACHE.
  • The commit each source was read at is written to the coverage file (the ODD's sources), and scenario-coverage lists it, warning when the merged runs read different commits of a source.

From Python, pass GitSource(url, rev, path) to load_openodd().

docs.title: What is read
docs.text:
IMPORT: other files, relative to the importing one, or else in the other sources (see above). A cycle is refused.

Every file read with an ODD makes up one transmission, in the standard's words, and the standard makes two things unique within one. Both are refused rather than guessed at:

  • two different files of the same name, wherever they come from;
  • a concept defined in two files, even the same way. A file can still add concepts to a container another file started (weather: in both, with different concepts under it).

TAXONOMY: nested mappings are records and containers. A leaf is one of:

  • integer|long|float|double <unit type>: a number;
  • boolean;
  • a list of literals: a categorical;
  • a mapping of literals to expressions on other concepts: a categorical defined by them. Its value is the literal whose expressions hold; on a shared range endpoint, the literal written first wins. Defined by ranges, its literals are ordered in the order written, so "< heavy_rain" means the literals before it;
  • the id of a categorical: the same literals.

A reference to a record (a user-defined type) and a shapefile are not followed.

MODULES and ODD: modules. Those under ODD are the root candidates: the ones among them no other module refers to are the roots. The standard's examples also put referenced modules there. Without an ODD section, every module no other module refers to is a root.

A module's keys are:

  • TITLE, DESCRIPTION;
  • ACTIVE;
  • LABEL / LABELS (one name or a list);
  • METADATA (ignored, here and inside a section);
  • one INCLUDE_AND or INCLUDE_OR, and one EXCLUDE_AND or EXCLUDE_OR.

A section nests one level of the other operator: OR: in an AND section, AND: in an OR one.

A section maps a concept to an expression, or a module or label to true/false. A concept is named by its id (wind_speed), or by as much of its path as makes it unique.

Expression Meaning low, 3, true, "0 mm/h" equal [a, b] one of the literals "> x unit", ">= x", "< x", "<= x" a bound (> excludes x, >= includes it) "[low .. high] unit", "[low, high] unit" an inclusive range "< literal", "[a .. b]" a bound or range over an ordered categorical unknown (none, null, undefined, or YAML null) the value is missing, unless the categorical has a literal of that name

A number's unit must measure the concept's unit type. It is converted into the probe's unit, so "> 50 km/h" against a probe in m/s is > 13.89. The units known are listed below; a document adds more with OpenODD's conversion: block.

Unit type Units length m, km, cm, mm, mi, in, ft velocity m/s, km/h (kph), mph acceleration m/s^2, g time s, ms (msec), min, h angle deg, rad precipitation_rate mm/h (mm/hr) temperature C, K, F fraction % bandwidth bps, kbps, Mbps, Gbps frequency Hz, kHz illuminance lx count, occurrence count, 1/h, occ/hr

The following are refused, each with the module it appears in:

  • a concept that is not in the taxonomy;
  • a literal a categorical does not have;
  • a unit of the wrong type;
  • a second include or exclude section;
  • deeper nesting;
  • a module or label id containing unknown.

The YAML is read with YAML 1.2 booleans: only true and false are booleans, so literals such as off or NO stay literals. A key written twice is refused. As the standard notes, an unquoted expression starting with > (speed: > 50 km/h) is a YAML block scalar, so quote it.

Not read: COD / OD records, numeric terms (1.75*ego_width), $ parameters, and condition-level metadata.

docs.title: The binding file
docs.text:
Key Meaning openodd The OpenODD files, relative to the binding file name, text The ODD's name and description probes Concept → probe (built-in name or package.module:function) or measure (a scenario measure's key, see Scenario measures), unit (built-in probes and measures know theirs), buckets (values, buckets, or range + every), text, and the coverage criteria target, cover_by, min_stay situations Module → its criteria (target, cover_by, min_stay, all optional): the modules to cover as situations (see Situations above) 
situations:
  three_lane_cruise: {cover_by: meters, target: 200, min_stay: 3}
  urban_junction_rain: {}          # one stay of any length

Situations live in the binding file, not in the OpenODD documents: OpenODD has no notion of coverage, and a construct of its own in an OpenODD document would not be compliant. A module named under situations and not under the ODD section is not a root candidate.

When no buckets are given:

  • a categorical gets one bucket per literal, and a boolean gets two;
  • a number gets buckets at the thresholds the modules test it against. "<= 60 km/h" makes [-inf, 60) and [60, inf], so every boundary the ODD draws is tested from both sides. Each bucket holds its lower edge, so [60, inf] holds 60, which <= 60 lets in. That bucket is partly inside, so it stays a coverage target. With "< 60 km/h", it would be outside.

A categorical defined by expressions is measured when what its expressions read is. A concept with no probe is always missing, and is reported as monitored but not covered.

docs.title: Picking the ODD of a run
docs.text:
The odd config key, or ScenarioQueue(odd=...) / ScenarioRunner(odd=...), takes one of:

Value ODD default The built-in one (Coverage): every attribute, no modules. It is openodd's bundled default ODD (its files), measured by this framework's probes, so it has a revision like any ODD read from files a name One registered with register_odd(name, builder) in code, or by a package through the autoware_carla_scenario.odds entry point group (or openodd's openodd.odds) path/to/urban.yaml A binding file (or an OpenODD file on its own, measuring nothing) package.module:function A builder to import and call 
uv run scenario scenario=intersection_passing/left_turn odd=path/to/urban.yaml
uv run scenario scenario=intersection_passing/left_turn odd=my_package.odds:urban_odd

A package that ships its ODD registers it through the autoware_carla_scenario.odds entry point group, or openodd's openodd.odds when the ODD is not CARLA's alone (both are read; openodd.resolve_odd() resolves names as resolve_odd() does, with files measured by its backend). The entry point names a function that takes nothing and calls register_odd, the convention the scenario and traffic-backend groups use. A private taxonomy can then plug in without the framework knowing it:

[project.entry-points."autoware_carla_scenario.odds"]
my_package = "my_package.odds:register"

def register() -> None:
    register_odd("urban", urban_odd)

docs.title: Sampling scenarios from the ODD
docs.text:
Coverage says which situations of the ODD the runs so far have driven. The sampler draws the settings of the next runs from the ODD: only combinations the ODD admits, and, if asked, aimed at what is still uncovered. It is a sweep, so it is run by scenario-expand and by the lanelet sweeper, and with autoware.launcher each case gets a fresh Autoware (Autoware as the Ego):

uv run scenario --multirun hydra/sweeper=lanelet_constraint \
  scenario=intersection_passing/left_turn map=town10hd_opt \
  +sweep.odd_sample.count=20 +sweep.odd_sample.strategy=coverage \
  '+sweep.odd_sample.coverage_from=[outputs]'

A glob batch with --multirun draws each matched scenario's cases the same way and runs them all in one queue (Batch Execution). Scenarios that draw from one ODD go on from each other's draws, in the order the batch lists them: with strategy: coverage a later scenario counts the earlier ones' cases as covered and aims at the buckets and situations they left (see How a case is drawn); with strategy: uniform it draws from a random stream of its own rather than repeat their values. Here cut_in/right's 3 cases aim at what cut_in/left's 3 left uncovered:

uv run scenario --multirun 'scenario=cut_in/*' map=town10hd_opt \
  +sweep.odd_sample.count=3 +sweep.odd_sample.strategy=coverage

The same seed, ODD, knobs, coverage and scenarios, in the same order, give the same cases, on any machine (openodd's sampler draws from ChaCha8 seeded with the seed's SHA-256). Two ODDs are one when they are built alike (their structure), however the command line names them (a registered name, a YAML path); a scenario on another ODD starts afresh.

or in the scenario's YAML:

sweep:
  odd_sample:
    count: 20              # cases; one per lanelet case when left out
    seed: 0                # same seed, ODD, knobs and coverage: same cases
    strategy: coverage     # uniform | coverage
    coverage_from: [outputs]   # earlier runs' *_coverage.json (files or directories)
    odd: null              # the ODD to draw from; the run's (`odd`) by default
    knobs: {}              # by ODD attribute, replacing the scenario's controls; see below
    flaky: null            # look for flaky cases; see "Finding flaky cases" below
    tire_friction: true    # draw each case's grip in the range its weather allows; see "Tire friction follows the weather"
    visibility: true       # draw how far each case's drivers see in the range its weather allows; see "Visibility follows the weather"

Each case is a list of Hydra overrides. A sweep that also has constraints gives each drawn case the next lanelet case in turn; one without draws from the ODD alone, and needs no map to expand. The last override, ++odd_case=..., is the case itself, encoded: the run records it, with its outcome, in its coverage file (see Finding flaky cases).

docs.title: Who knows what
docs.text:
Three things meet in a sampled case, and none of them knows the others:

Says Knows The ODD which conditions the system is for, and which scenario measure each of its attributes is (its mapping) its taxonomy and the measure keys; no scenario A scenario its measures (BaseScenario's, or its own replacements) and its controls: which of its parameters sets which measure, and what it can stage the measure keys; not the ODD's taxonomy or bounds The framework the measure keys, and the weather and sun every scenario can be given neither

An ODD tightened, loosened or written in another taxonomy needs no scenario changed; a scenario added needs no ODD changed. The sampler joins them on the measure key: an attribute the ODD maps onto measure k is drawn with the running scenario's control of k. Attributes nothing sets are left open: a combination is admitted when the ODD can hold for some value of them. Controls of measures the ODD does not map are unused -- what the ODD does not speak of, it does not bound.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
A control (an OddKnob) ties a measure to the config key that sets it. A scenario declares its own in its config, next to the parameters they set, keyed by measure:

# scenario/cut_in/left.yaml
controls:
  vehicle_ahead_gap_m:
    key: scenario.npc_gap_m
    target: measure                    # the gap the measure reads at the start
    range: [2.0, 30.0]                 # what the scenario can stage
  vehicle_ahead_relative_speed_kph:
    key: scenario.npc_initial_speed_kmh
    offset: ${ego.initial_speed_kmh}   # its speed less the ego's
    range: [-15.0, 15.0]
    limits: [0.0, null]                # a speed: never below zero, however slow the ego
Field Meaning key The config key the value is written to target setting (the default): the key is a raw setting, written through scale and offset. measure: the key takes the measure's value at the start itself, written unchanged -- no scale, offset, integer or values (see below) range Numeric: [low, high] in the measure's unit, the values the scenario can bring about. A bucket is drawn only where it meets the range (by more than an edge), and only that part of it values Per bucket label. Categorical: the value to write, or [low, high) to draw it from ([x, x] is x); a bucket without one is not drawn. Numeric: a range to draw from instead of the bucket's interval -- which an unbounded bucket (-inf/inf edges) needs to be drawn at all scale, offset A numeric value drawn in the unit is written as value * scale + offset (scale not zero) integer Write an integer. A rounded numeric value that falls in another bucket is drawn again limits Numeric: [low, high] the written value must lie in, null for an open end -- what the key takes, whatever offset comes to. A bucket only values outside it would reach is not drawn

{measure: key} is short for {measure: {key: key}}. The ODD's attribute and the measure share a unit: the binding takes the measure's.

docs.title: Raw settings and measure-targeted controls
docs.text:
A raw setting (target: setting) is a scenario parameter the drawn value is mapped onto by scale and offset, and the mapping is the author's claim that the parameter brings the measure about. It holds where the two are the same quantity by definition. It is a guess where they are not: npc_ahead_m is the NPC's s along its lanelet less the ego's along its own, while vehicle_ahead_gap_m is bumper to bumper along the ego's lane. Neighbouring lanelets do not run alike on a curve -- the outer one is longer, and their s do not line up -- and the bumpers depend on the vehicles, so no constant offset is right wherever the scenario is placed (on CARLA 0.10 Town04_Opt one guessed +11 m was measured 2.2 m off, and the right offset there is right nowhere else).

A measure that the initial placement alone determines can be the parameter instead. The scenario takes "the measure should read v at the start" and solves for the placement that makes it so, evaluating the measure's own definition on the poses it will spawn at; the control says target: measure, and the value drawn is written unchanged:

from autoware_carla_scenario import place_at_vehicle_ahead_gap, vehicle_bumpers

# The NPC's s on its lanelet at which vehicle_ahead_gap_m reads cfg.npc_gap_m,
# seen from where the ego spawns -- whatever the two lanelets' shapes.
ego_at = to_carla_world(self._spawn_pose).to_carla_transform()
npc_pose = place_at_vehicle_ahead_gap(
    ego_at,
    cfg.npc_lanelet_id,
    cfg.npc_gap_m,
    ego_bumpers=vehicle_bumpers(world, self.ego_config.vehicle_type),
    npc_bumpers=vehicle_bumpers(world, cfg.npc_vehicle_type),
)

place_at_vehicle_ahead_gap reads the gap with the measure's own code (measures.vehicle_ahead_gap_between, which the measure reads every vehicle with) for the NPC at each s of its lanelet, as a Lanelet2Pose spawns there -- on the centreline, heading along it -- and narrows the first crossing of v down by bisection (solve_along, a 1-D root find that takes any s -> measure function, for a measure of a scenario's own). It solves on the NPC's own lanelet and projects the NPC onto the ego's lane, so it does not matter where the lanelets beside each other start or how long they are. A gap the lanelet cannot reach -- too short, turning away, or out of the lanes the measure counts -- is refused with the gaps it does reach, so a drawn case that cannot be staged fails at setup rather than running another gap.

The gap is bumper to bumper, so the placement needs both vehicles' sizes before either is spawned. CARLA gives a blueprint no size: vehicle_bumpers reads the bounding box of a vehicle of the blueprint already in the world when there is one, and otherwise spawns one high above the map (higher again if that spawn is refused), reads its bounding box and destroys it before the world ticks again -- once per blueprint per process. The vehicle-ahead measures do not count a vehicle that far above the ego. The NPC is then spawned once, where the gap reads right, rather than spawned, measured and moved -- a move that would race its initial speed and the first tick.

Which to use:

The measure is Control decided by where and how road users start, and the parameter is that measure by definition (npc_initial_speed_kmh less the ego's is the relative speed) a raw setting, with the offset that makes it the measure decided by where road users start, but the parameter is another quantity (an arc length for a gap) target: measure, with the scenario solving its placement decided by what the run then drives (a pedestrian's gap when it sets off, anything a controller or traffic changes) a raw setting; how far the measure drifts from what was drawn is read off the runs, in openodd's case plot (its drift/calibration view), not solved at setup

The relative speed of cut_in is the first kind: both vehicles start at their speeds along their lanes, and the measure is the NPC's velocity along the ego's lane at the NPC less the ego's along it at the ego, so its offset: ${ego.initial_speed_kmh} writes it exactly: on a bend the NPC heads along its lane, which runs alongside the ego's lane where it is. (A lane beside a bend is shorter or longer than the ego's, so an NPC on it covers the ego's lane a few per cent slower or faster -- 3.5 m off a 100 m radius, 3.5 % -- which the measure does not count: it reads speeds, not how fast s changes.)

The weather and the sun are set for every scenario, through the environment config, which sets them before the run starts (EnvironmentAction); the built-in probes reading them have controls of their own:

Probe Key Ranges rain environment.rain none 0, light 1-30, moderate 30-70, heavy 70-100 fog environment.fog_density as rain illumination environment.sun_altitude_angle day 15-90, low_sun 0-15, twilight -6-0, night -90 to -6 visibility environment.visibility_m 15-400 m, whatever the weather

environment.rain sets the precipitation and, with it, the cloudiness, standing water and wetness of CARLA's rain presets (EnvironmentAction's rain): precipitation alone draws only the falling drops, and a camera sees a dry road under a clear sky. The probe reads the precipitation, so a drawn value still reads back as its bucket. rain and precipitation cannot both be set (the run fails at its start), and the none bucket, rain=0, is a dry road under a clear sky whatever the map's own weather.

Fog is drawn as fog_density alone. How thick that looks is the server's: a CARLA 0.10 server on the UE 5.8 engine (the ue58-dev tree) multiplies it by carla.Weather.FogDensityScale, whose default 0.001 leaves even fog_density=100 a faint haze on the horizon. Start it with -ExecCmds="carla.Weather.FogDensityScale 0.01" for fog a camera sees, or set server.fog_density_scale=0.01 (LiDAR).

The rain and fog knobs set the LiDAR noise as well: each driver.lidars sweep carries the world's precipitation and fog density (LiDAR).

A scenario that sets the weather itself (its own EnvironmentAction) has the last word over the config.

docs.title: Tire friction follows the weather
docs.text:
CARLA draws rain but does not drive on it: a vehicle grips a soaked road as it grips a dry one. So an EnvironmentAction that sets the road's water -- rain, wetness or precipitation_deposits -- also scales every vehicle's wheel friction (friction_force_multiplier) to a share of the dry road's grip, within the range the resulting weather leaves (tire_friction_range), by the larger of wetness and precipitation_deposits:

Road water Grip, share of the dry road's What rain gives it 0 (dry) 0.90-1.10 rain=0 50 (wet) 0.65-0.85 rain=30 (standing water 50) 100 (flooded) 0.45-0.65 rain=100

Between the rows the bounds are interpolated. Measured tire-road friction is about 0.8-1.0 on dry asphalt, 0.5-0.7 on wet and 0.3-0.5 under a water film; each range spans what tires, their wear and the asphalt make of the same water, and a dry road's is centred on CARLA's own grip, so a dry run drives as it did before.

Where in the range a run's grip is, is environment.tire_friction_quantile (0 its low end, 1 its high end; the middle when not set). A sweep.odd_sample draws it for every case (environment.tire_friction_quantile=0.412 among the case's overrides, recorded in its coverage file), from the sweep's seed and the case, so the same sweep draws the same grip. The weather comes from the ODD and the grip from the range that weather allows: a heavy-rain case never runs on a dry road's grip. tire_friction: false in the odd_sample leaves every case at the middle of its range, and environment.tire_friction fixes the grip whatever the weather (it wins over the quantile).

The vehicles in the world when the action fires are scaled then; a scenario with such an action -- the config's, or its own -- also runs follow_tire_friction after every tick, which gives the vehicles spawned later (background traffic) the same grip. A scenario that sets the weather on the tick loop sets the grip with it: a factor applied again replaces the last one rather than compounding it.

The example scenarios declare these:

Scenario Measure Parameter cut_in/* vehicle_ahead_gap_m npc_gap_m (target: measure), 2-30 m cut_in/* vehicle_ahead_relative_speed_kph npc_initial_speed_kmh less the ego's, -15 to 15 km/h pedestrian_dart_out crossing_pedestrian_gap_m trigger_distance_m, 8-30 m pedestrian_dart_out crossing_pedestrian_speed_ms walk_speed_ms, 0.8-3 m/s

traffic_light_compliance declares none, but has what a control needs: stop_line_distance_m (target: measure: the ego is moved along the lane its spawn pose is on until stop_line_distance_m reads it, place_at_stop_line_distance), and its own measure red_light_duration_s, the seconds every light is held red (light_switch_delay_seconds, a raw setting). With the delay drawn, timeout_after_green_seconds counts the fail-safe timeout from the green light instead of from the start. A drawn distance does not decide the verdict by itself: the run is judged by where the ego stops against that same line -- not past it on red, standing in the stop zone (stop_zone_min_m-stop_zone_max_m before it) by the green -- so an ego started far back may roll up to the line on red.

sweep.odd_sample.knobs takes the same fields keyed by the ODD's attributes, and replaces anything above, attribute by attribute, for that sweep. It is for the command line -- one sweep against one ODD -- not for a scenario's config, which would then name the ODD's taxonomy: a scenario says controls. Controls set where a run starts; the measures read what it then drives, which is what coverage counts.

docs.title: Visibility follows the weather
docs.text:
CARLA draws the weather but its traffic never looks through it: the TrafficManager's vehicles know where every actor is, fog or not. A driver does not, and drives so as to stop within the road they see. So how far drivers see is a quantity of the run, in metres, which the weather bounds (visibility_range, in autoware_carla_scenario.visibility): each of the fog, the rain and the light gives a range, and the shortest holds.

Weather Visibility, m clear day 250-400 fog_density 30 / 70 / 100 120-250 / 40-100 / 15-40 precipitation 30 / 70 / 100 180-320 / 100-220 / 60-150 night (sun_altitude_angle -6 and below) 50-150 (a dipped beam to a main beam or a lit street)

Between the rows the bounds are interpolated; through civil twilight (0 to -6 degrees) the day's range shortens to the night's. An EnvironmentAction that sets the fog, the rain (rain or precipitation) or the sun records the visibility of the weather it leaves for its world, at environment.visibility_quantile in that range (0 its low end, 1 its high end; the middle when not set); environment.visibility_m fixes it whatever the weather. A sweep.odd_sample draws the quantile for every case, as it draws the grip, so the ODD's rain, fog and illumination knobs are what shorten it: a night case's drivers see 50-150 m, a heavy-fog case's 15-40 m. visibility: false in the odd_sample leaves every case at the middle of its range. An ODD that names the visibility itself (the visibility probe) sets it through its own knob, environment.visibility_m, and a case with one keeps it. A run that sets no weather records none, and its traffic sees as it always did; each run starts with none, whatever the last left.

What follows it is the traffic backend's: the sumo backend holds its own traffic to the speed it stops from within it (Visibility); the TrafficManager has no notion of sight, so the traffic_manager backend logs the speed it would hold traffic to whenever the visibility changes, and its vehicles drive as before.

docs.title: The road a case is on
docs.text:
A sweep with cases of its own -- constraints, or a route search -- draws the attributes the Lanelet2 map decides as well: whether the case is in a junction, how many lanes, the speed limit, the location and road type tags. Each is read off every case's lanelet (its first *lanelet_id override: the constraints' pick, or the route's spawn) with the probe's lanelet form, and gets a knob that reaches the buckets those lanelets are in. The knobs write no setting a run reads (_odd_map.*, taken off again); instead each drawn case is put on a case whose lanelet is in every bucket drawn, the one run least so far among those that are. So a lanelet case may run more than once, or not at all, even without a count: the buckets decide, not the list of cases. Each run records its case (++odd_case) with its own lanelet's buckets and values, not the ones drawn.

Not every combination of buckets is on one lanelet -- no junction where the limit is 30, say -- and each knob draws its attribute on its own, so 20 cases are drawn for each one kept and those no lanelet fits are passed over. If too few fit, the rest go on the lanelet in most of their buckets, with a warning. So strategy: coverage aims at the road as at everything else: the buckets of junction, lane count or speed limit that earlier runs left uncovered come first, as far as the sweep's cases reach them.

A sweep that gives an attribute a knob itself (odd_sample.knobs) keeps it. The flaky search (odd_sample.flaky) draws its cases as it chooses them, none passed over; each goes on the lanelet in most of its buckets.

docs.title: How a case is drawn
docs.text:
1. Each knob's attribute gets one of its buckets, leaving out the buckets outside the ODD (the ones scenario-odd show lists as out).
  2. The combination is kept only if the ODD's verdict on those buckets is not outside -- so modules that rule out a combination (no heavy rain at night, say) are honoured, not just single buckets.
  3. A value is drawn inside each bucket (a numeric bucket's interval, or the knob's range) and checked against the ODD again, as a value, with the attributes an OpenODD ODD derives from others worked out: a condition finer than a bucket (between(0, 45) across a [30, 60) bucket) holds for what is drawn. What is written is the value exactly as drawn, and a numeric one is read back to check it is still in its bucket.

strategy: uniform draws every admitted bucket alike. strategy: coverage reads coverage_from and draws each attribute from its least covered buckets first, counting the cases already drawn in the batch -- by earlier scenarios on the same ODD too, in a glob batch -- as covered, so a batch works through the holes before it repeats one; it falls back to any bucket (the less covered the likelier) only when the ODD admits no combination of the least covered. Situations that are still holes (or that no earlier run measured) are aimed at first, one case each; inactive ones are not, nor are those an earlier case of the batch was aimed at. A situation the knobs alone decide -- every attribute it tests has a knob, and it refers to no other module -- holds in its case. One that also tests what no knob sets -- a speed, a road -- gets a case under which it can hold; whether it does is up to the drive. A situation the ODD and the knobs leave no case for is given up on, with a warning.

coverage_from paths are relative to the directory the sweep is started from. Coverage is read when the sweep is expanded: to resume a sweep (sweep.resume_from) into the same cases, read the same coverage -- point coverage_from at the earlier runs, not at the sweep's own output.

From Python:

from pathlib import Path

from autoware_carla_scenario.coverage.report import load_and_merge
from autoware_carla_scenario.odd import OddKnob, OddSampler, resolve_odd

sampler = OddSampler(
    resolve_odd("path/to/urban.yaml"),
    controls={"vehicle_ahead_gap_m": OddKnob("scenario.npc_gap_m", range=(2.0, 30.0))},
    seed=0,
    strategy="coverage",
    coverage=load_and_merge([Path("outputs")]),
)
for case in sampler.sample(20):
    print(case.overrides, case.buckets, case.situation)

To go on from cases drawn before -- another scenario's, on the same ODD -- pass them as drawn; OddDraws keeps them per ODD, as a batch does:

from autoware_carla_scenario.odd import OddDraws

draws = OddDraws()
draws.add(sampler.odd, sampler.sample(20))
later = OddSampler(sampler.odd, seed=0, strategy="coverage", drawn=draws.of(sampler.odd))

docs.title: Finding flaky cases
docs.text:
Every run a sweep draws from the ODD records its case in its coverage file: the values it ran with, why it was drawn, and whether it passed (openodd's CoverageCollector.record_case and record_outcome; the runner calls them, so a scenario needs nothing of its own). The merged report then lists the runs, flakiest first, with their flakiness assessed over all the runs of their scenario (scenario-coverage, section Flaky cases).

With flaky, the sweep also looks for them. openodd's FlakySearch learns where the runs in coverage_from passed and failed (Gaussian-process classification), and draws part of each batch where a small change would flip the outcome -- after the sampler has covered every bucket, the rest of the batch still sweeping the ODD (openodd's docs/flaky.md):

sweep:
  odd_sample:
    count: 20
    strategy: coverage
    coverage_from: [outputs]       # the earlier sweeps' runs: what the search learns from
    flaky:
      explore_fraction: 0.8        # of each batch, once every bucket is covered
      scenario: CutInScenario      # learn from this scenario's runs only (all, when left out)

flaky: true takes the defaults. Its other fields are FlakySearch's: pool, coverage_depth, threshold, epsilon, perturbations, draws and directions. Only runs drawn in the same space -- the same attributes, ranges and labels -- with an outcome are learnt from; a sweep with no such run draws all its cases with the sampler's own policy. Each case chosen for its instability records the flakiness predicted for it, beside the one the report assesses. Run the sweeps one after another, each reading the earlier ones' outputs, and every sweep looks where the last left the outcome unsure.

docs.title: Checking an ODD
docs.text:
uv run scenario-odd check my_package.odds:urban_odd   # compile with Codon
uv run scenario-odd check path/to/urban.yaml          # read the binding and OpenODD files
uv run scenario-odd show path/to/urban.yaml           # attributes, buckets in and out
uv run scenario-odd list                              # ODDs known by name

check compiles a Python ODD with Codon, the same way a scenario is compiled. It catches the following:

  • a misspelt name;
  • a condition of the wrong type (between("0", 60));
  • a probe that does not take a world.

The runner makes the same check before a run, under the typecheck config key. OpenODD YAML is checked as it is read (see What is read).

docs.title: Checking a planned route
docs.text:
Before a scenario runs, its ego route can be checked against the ODD on the Lanelet2 map alone, with no CARLA server:

uv run scenario-odd route path/to/urban.yaml intersection_passing/left_turn
uv run scenario-odd route urban 'intersection_passing/*' lane_change/left map=nishishinjuku
uv run scenario-odd route urban 'lane_change/*' --json

Each scenario config is composed as a run composes it. Name it as scenario= does (a glob works too); arguments with an = are Hydra overrides for all of them. The route is planned from the ego's spawn pose (ego.spawn_lanelet_id, ego.spawn_s), through ego.waypoint_lanelet_ids, to the goal (ego.goal_lanelet_id, ego.goal_s), as the shortest path in the map's routing graph, leg by leg. A scenario that derives its goal in setup() from scenario.expected_route_lanelet_ids, as intersection_passing does, gets that goal here too (a configured goal wins). A goal derived any other way is only known once the scenario runs: that route is reported as not planned.

The ODD's attributes are then read lanelet by lanelet along the route, and each lanelet gets one of three verdicts:

Verdict Meaning inside The ODD holds there, whatever happens at run time. outside The ODD fails there, whatever happens at run time. Reported with the lanelet ids and the modules that fail. undecided It depends on what only the run can tell (weather, traffic, speed), or on a value the map does not have. At run time a missing value counts as inside, so this is "inside only by assumption".

The map decides an attribute when its probe has a lanelet form, probe.on_lanelet(lanelet, lanelet_map, routing_graph). It returns the value, None where the run would read none, or UNDECIDED where only the run can tell (for example speed_limit_kph on a lanelet with no speed_limit tag, where the run falls back to CARLA's limit). The built-in probes listed above have one; a custom probe opts in by having an on_lanelet attribute (a function attribute, or a method of a callable object). An attribute whose probe has none is open: it could take any value, and the ODD's own three-valued evaluation decides, exactly as it does for buckets outside the ODD. An OpenODD attribute derived from others is worked out from their values on the lanelet, and is open while one of them is.

What the lanelet forms read, and where that differs from the run:

Probe On a lanelet At run time in_junction The lanelet has a turn_direction tag (Autoware tags every lanelet in an intersection with one; the sweeper's is_junction reads it the same way) CARLA waypoint is_junction lane_count The lanelet and every same-direction neighbour, walked left and right in the routing graph (left/right, else adjacentLeft/adjacentRight, so lanes behind a solid line count too); nothing in a junction CARLA OpenDRIVE waypoints: driving lanes of the same sign speed_limit_kph The speed_limit tag, else (no tag, or not a number) undecided The tag, else CARLA's get_speed_limit() lanelet_location, lanelet_subtype, lanelet_speed_limit_kph The tag The tag of the lanelet the ego is on

Route lane counts come from Lanelet2 and run-time lane counts come from CARLA's OpenDRIVE waypoints. The two maps are converted from each other but not always lane for lane, so they can disagree; so can the two junction criteria.

The report also gives the expected coverage: the metres the route spends in each bucket of each attribute (<undecided> and <missing> collect the metres where the map cannot or does not say). The start lanelet counts from the spawn pose, the goal lanelet up to the goal pose, and a lane change splits the lanelets' length between the two sides. Over several scenarios the metres are summed, and the report lists the buckets of each map-decided attribute that no planned route reaches, leaving out buckets outside the ODD (they are not targets). An attribute the map decides in general but left undecided on some lanelet of a route (metres in <undecided>) is reported as undetermined instead: the run may reach any of its buckets there, so none is called unreached.

The exit status is 0 when no route leaves the ODD, 1 when one does, and 2 when a route could not be planned (no goal, no path, a lanelet the map does not have, no Lanelet2 map) or the ODD could not be read.

From Python:

from autoware_carla_scenario.odd import (
    PlannedRoute, combine_route_coverage, plan_route_coverage,
)
from autoware_carla_scenario.coordinate import Lanelet2Pose

route = PlannedRoute(start=Lanelet2Pose(203, 25.0), goal=Lanelet2Pose(207, 10.0))
coverage = plan_route_coverage("urban", route, lanelet_map=lanelet_map)
coverage.leaves_odd, coverage.outside(), coverage.expected_m
combine_route_coverage("urban", [coverage, ...]).unreached

plan_route_coverage also takes a scenario (its spawn pose, waypoints and goal) or a list of lanelet ids. Without lanelet_map it uses the map the runner has loaded.

At start-up, once setup() has settled the goal, the runner plans the route the same way and logs a warning when it leaves the ODD. It is a warning only. It is skipped for an ODD with no modules, and anything that keeps the route from being planned is logged at debug level; the run goes on regardless.

docs.title: What the report says
docs.text:
For each ODD the merged runs were measured against, scenario-coverage says the following (Coverage):

  • how long the runs were inside it, inside only because values were missing, and outside it;
  • which modules ruled ticks out, and how often, and how often their verdict rested on missing values;
  • which runs left it, and when (the first intervals);
  • which attributes are monitored but not covered.

A bucket is outside the ODD when the ODD fails for every value in it, whatever the other attributes are. It is reported, but it is not a coverage target. An example is nonurban under location.is_in(["urban"]).

To decide this, the ODD's own evaluation runs with the bucket in place of the attribute's value and every other attribute left open. Labels, inactive modules, groups and module references therefore count exactly as they do on a tick. A condition that ties attributes together (any_of across two of them, or a junction and a speed) rules out combinations, never a single bucket. A bucket only partly inside ([60, 90] under <= 60) stays a target.

docs.title: Quick start: test a driving policy
docs.text:
From an empty directory to a scenario result, with no ROS 2 and no Autoware. The framework downloads CARLA, launches it, serves the driving policy in its own process and runs the scenario: after the setup it is one command.

You need Linux x86_64, uv, git, an NVIDIA GPU that runs CARLA UE5, and about 30 GB of free disk for the simulator. (The framework also runs on Linux aarch64, but CARLA's server does not: there, run CARLA on an x86_64 host and add server.host=<address> to the commands below; see installation.)

docs.title: 1. Add the framework to your project
docs.text:
The framework is a Python library on PyPI. Depend on it from your project's pyproject.toml:

[project]
name = "my-policy-tests"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.15"
dependencies = ["autoware-carla-scenario>=5"]

uv sync

This also installs carla-driver-interface 1.x, the policy side of the gRPC contract (versioned on its own; a policy depending on any 1.x shares the environment), and the CARLA client, typesafe_carla. Its wheel carries a prebuilt CPython package. Where that package does not match the installed toolchain, the first run that imports the client builds it once instead (15-50 min, ~14 GB of memory, needs cc) into ~/.cache/typesafe_carla. uv run typesafe-codon pycarla does that ahead of time, and says "nothing to build" when the prebuilt package applies.

docs.title: 2. Download CARLA
docs.text:
uv run scenario-setup

This downloads CARLA's nightly Linux build (about 16 GB, with a progress bar) and unpacks it, while it downloads, into ~/.autoware_carla_scenario/bin/carla. That is where the scenario runner looks for CARLA when CARLA_EXECUTABLE is not set. Run it again at any time: an install that is still the current nightly is kept, a newer one replaces it. If the connection drops partway, the download picks up where it stopped (with an HTTP range request) instead of starting over; it gives up after several reconnections in a row that deliver nothing, and stops (the next run fetches it whole) if the nightly was replaced in the meantime.

Option Meaning --force Download again even if the install is current --url URL Install another CARLA Linux package (.tar.gz), e.g. a release --dir DIR Unpack into DIR (new or empty) instead; then point CARLA_EXECUTABLE at the launcher it prints

AUTOWARE_CARLA_SCENARIO_HOME moves ~/.autoware_carla_scenario as a whole.

docs.title: 3. Run a scenario against a policy
docs.text:
uv run scenario scenario=cut_in/left map=town10hd_opt \
  ego.spawn_lanelet_id=324 scenario.npc_lanelet_id=446 \
  ego.entity=carla_driver driver.policy=route_follower

The single command does everything:

  1. It launches CARLA (CarlaUnreal.sh, on server.port). The first boot takes a minute or two. A CARLA already listening on that port is used instead.
  2. It fetches the Town10HD_Opt Lanelet2 map into ~/autoware_data/maps, the first time only.
  3. It serves route_follower, a reference policy, inside the scenario's own process.
  4. It runs the scenario, prints the pass/fail result, writes it under outputs/, and stops CARLA again.

ego.entity=carla_driver hands the ego to a policy over alpasim's egodriver.EgodriverService contract. driver.policy names the policy the scenario serves itself.

The example scenarios name lanelets of the NishishinjukuMap by default, so on Town10HD_Opt a run gives its own. The two above are one of the cases the scenario's sweep matches. scenario-expand lists every case, each as the overrides to add to the command above, without running anything:

uv run scenario-expand scenario=cut_in/left map=town10hd_opt

docs.title: 4. Test your own policy
docs.text:
A policy implements BaseDriver.drive(). It gets the session's observations and returns a trajectory in the rig frame (x forward, y left):

# src/my_policy_tests/__init__.py
from carla_driver_interface.driver import BaseDriver, DriveContext, DriveResult
from carla_driver_interface.geometry import Pose, Trajectory


class MyPolicy(BaseDriver):
    name = "my_policy"

    def drive(self, ctx: DriveContext) -> DriveResult:
        plan = Trajectory.empty()
        for i in range(1, 41):  # 4 s ahead at 5 m/s
            plan.append(ctx.time_now_us + i * 100_000, Pose.from_xyz_yaw(0.5 * i, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
        return DriveResult(trajectory_in_rig=plan)

So that uv sync installs the module, give the project a build backend:

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.9.7,<0.10.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

Then name the policy by its import path:

uv run scenario scenario=cut_in/left map=town10hd_opt \
  ego.spawn_lanelet_id=324 scenario.npc_lanelet_id=446 \
  ego.entity=carla_driver driver.policy=my_policy_tests:MyPolicy

See External Driver Interface for what a policy receives (cameras, LiDAR, the map, traffic lights). Other scenarios are listed in Example Scenarios.

docs.title: Running the policy as a separate process
docs.text:
A policy can also live in a process of its own, for example an alpasim driver or a model in another environment. Leave driver.policy unset and point driver.address at it:

# Terminal 1 -- the policy
uv run carla-driver-interface serve --policy my_policy_tests:MyPolicy --port 50051

# Terminal 2 -- the scenario
uv run scenario scenario=cut_in/left map=town10hd_opt \
  ego.spawn_lanelet_id=324 scenario.npc_lanelet_id=446 \
  ego.entity=carla_driver driver.address=localhost:50051

Both modes use the same gRPC contract and the same policy class. The only difference is which process serves the policy.

docs.title: ROS 2 over DDS
docs.text:
ego.entity=ros2 hands the ego to ROS 2 nodes directly over DDS. The framework joins the DDS domain itself, through Cyclone DDS's Python binding: no rclpy, no ROS 2 installation, no bridge node and no gRPC. It publishes the ego's state on ROS 2 topics, takes commands from them, and applies the one that drives.

It takes the place of the CARLA-to-ROS 2 bridge nodes a ROS 2 stack would otherwise run beside CARLA: the ego-state and speed publishers, and the arbiter that chooses between command sources.

flowchart LR
    subgraph scenario["Scenario process"]
        SR["ScenarioRunner<br/>ticks the world"]
        E["Ros2EgoEntity<br/>arbiter + controller"]
        SR -->|on_tick| E
        E -->|"VehicleControl /<br/>VehicleAckermannControl"| SR
    end
    subgraph ros["ROS 2 nodes (rmw_cyclonedds_cpp)"]
        P["planner / VisionPilot /<br/>safety island ..."]
    end
    CARLA["CARLA server<br/>(native ROS 2)"]
    E -->|"/localization/kinematic_state<br/>/vehicle/status/steering_status<br/>/vehicle/speed"| P
    P -->|"trajectory / control /<br/>steering + acceleration"| E
    CARLA -->|"camera, /clock<br/>(or the entity, for a server<br/>built without ROS 2)"| P

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
The DDS binding is the ros2 extra:

pip install 'autoware-carla-scenario[ros2]'

In this repository the dev group installs it too (uv sync --dev).

cyclonedds ships wheels for Linux x86_64 on CPython 3.10-3.13 only, and the extra installs nothing elsewhere; ego.entity=ros2 then fails at scenario start, saying so.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
uv run scenario ego.entity=ros2 server.max_tick_rate_hz=20

The ROS 2 nodes run with RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp on the same ros2.domain_id. Cyclone reads CYCLONEDDS_URI in the scenario process exactly as it does in a node, so the same configuration file (interfaces, peers, fragment size) applies to both.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
Nothing waits for a command. Every tick the entity publishes the ego's state, takes the commands that arrived since the previous tick, and applies the one that drives; the simulation goes at the pace server.max_tick_rate_hz sets, and a source that falls silent goes stale. Set server.max_tick_rate_hz=20 -- real time at the 0.05 s step -- when the nodes measure wall-clock deadlines: a lockstep that stopped the simulation to wait for them would starve exactly the timeouts they are there to check. This is how a ROS 2 bridge that relays to CARLA behaves (VisionPilot's runs the world in synchronous mode, paced to wall-clock 10 Hz, without waiting for a command).

ego.entity=ros2 without server.max_tick_rate_hz logs a warning: unpaced, the simulation outruns the nodes and their sources look stale.

Published stamps and the freshness of commands are both in simulation time, the time CARLA's /clock carries, which is what nodes with use_sim_time read.

docs.title: What the ego publishes
docs.text:
Setting Type Contents kinematic_state_topic (/localization/kinematic_state) nav_msgs/Odometry pose in frame_id, twist in child_frame_id steering_status_topic (/vehicle/status/steering_status) autoware_vehicle_msgs/SteeringReport front tyre angle, positive to the left speed_topic (/vehicle/speed) std_msgs/Float64 ground speed, m/s clock_topic (off) rosgraph_msgs/Clock for a CARLA server built without ROS 2 turn_indicators_report_topic (/vehicle/status/turn_indicators_status) autoware_vehicle_msgs/TurnIndicatorsReport the indicators the ego shows (hazard, both lit, reports as off, as the report has no hazard)

null leaves a topic unpublished. The pose is in the right-handed local frame -- CARLA's world with y flipped, as CARLA's own ROS 2 interface publishes it -- with its origin on the rear axle, Autoware's base_link (rear_axle_offset_m, derived from the wheel physics when null).

Cameras and /clock are CARLA's to publish when the server is built with ROS 2. For a server built without it, the entity publishes them as well:

Setting Type Contents clock_topic rosgraph_msgs/Clock the simulation time, every tick cameras[].topic sensor_msgs/Image each frame of a camera on the ego, bgra8, stamped with the simulation time it was rendered at

A camera in cameras takes the rendering and mount fields of a driver camera (image_width, image_height, fov, fps, position_x/y/z, roll, pitch, yaw, in CARLA's convention), plus its topic and frame_id. Its frames go out from the sensor's own thread as they are rendered, the way CARLA's own interface publishes them, and under the names a node already subscribes to:

ros2:
  clock_topic: /clock
  cameras:
    - logical_id: main_cam
      topic: /carla/hero/main_cam/image
      frame_id: main_cam
      image_width: 1280
      image_height: 720
      fov: 60.0
      fps: 10.0
      position_x: 1.25
      position_z: 1.58

docs.title: Where commands come from
docs.text:
ros2.sources lists the publishers the ego takes commands from:

kind Topics Applied by trajectory topic: autoware_planning_msgs/Trajectory the framework's trajectory follower (pure pursuit + Autoware's PID longitudinal controller on the trajectory's own speeds, through the powertrain model), as for an external driver policy control topic: autoware_control_msgs/Control CARLA's Ackermann controller; Autoware's steering (positive left) is negated into CARLA's (positive right) steer_accel steering_topic, acceleration_topic: std_msgs/Float64 CARLA's Ackermann controller, as VisionPilot's carla_control_publisher hands it: target speed speed + acceleration * speed_horizon_s

The turn indicators are not a source: whichever source drives, the newest autoware_vehicle_msgs/TurnIndicatorsCommand on turn_indicators_command_topic (/control/command/turn_indicators_cmd; null turns it off) lights the ego's indicators, leaving its other lights as they are, until another changes them. NO_COMMAND changes nothing.

A steer_accel command is complete once a fresh value has arrived on both topics, and each value is used once, so a node that publishes one of each per cycle drives once per cycle.

A trajectory's points are timed by header.stamp + time_from_start; one whose time_from_start does not increase (many planners leave it zero) is timed from its speeds instead.

docs.title: Arbitration
docs.text:
Every tick, of the sources whose last command arrived at most stale_s ago, the one with the highest priority drives; between equal priorities, the most recent command. Once every source is stale, on_stale decides: hold keeps applying the last command (what a relay node does when its upstream stops), brake brakes to a stop. Before any command has arrived, the ego is held on its brakes.

ros2:
  domain_id: 0
  on_stale: hold
  sources:
    - name: planner
      kind: trajectory
      topic: /planning/scenario_planning/trajectory
      priority: 0
      stale_s: 0.3
  control: {}     # trajectory-follower gains, as driver.control

docs.title: The Open AD Kit safety-island demo
docs.text:
ros2=visionpilot_safety_island is the bench side of the Open AD Kit CES 2027 demo (openadkit#157): VisionPilot steers and accelerates, and a fresh command from the safety island (the CR52, restamped onto domain 1) overrides it.

uv run scenario ros2=visionpilot_safety_island
Source Kind Topics Priority visionpilot steer_accel /vehicle/steering_cmd, /vehicle/throttle_cmd 0 safety_island control /control/trajectory_follower/control_cmd 10

It selects ego.entity: ros2 on VisionPilot's vehicle (a Lincoln MKZ), DDS domain 1, and server.max_tick_rate_hz: 20.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from autoware_carla_scenario.entity.ros2_entity import Ros2EgoEntity
from autoware_carla_scenario.ros2 import CommandSourceConfig, Ros2EgoConfig

scenario.ego_entity = Ros2EgoEntity(
    Ros2EgoConfig(
        domain_id=1,
        sources=(
            CommandSourceConfig(name="planner", kind="trajectory",
                                topic="/planning/scenario_planning/trajectory"),
        ),
    )
)

To test without DDS, pass transport=FakeRos2Transport(config) and queue commands with its deliver().

docs.title: How it speaks ROS 2
docs.text: A node on rmw_cyclonedds_cpp publishes a message as a DDS sample of a type named <package>::msg::dds_::<Message>_ on the topic rt/<name>. autoware_carla_scenario.ros2.messages declares the same structs, field for field from the .msg definitions, so the samples are wire compatible with no ROS 2 type support installed. They are written in XCDR1, the representation rmw_cyclonedds_cpp writes.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Only rmw_cyclonedds_cpp has been tried. Other RMWs speak the same RTPS, but matching them is not tested.
  • The ego's role name is Ego, where VisionPilot subscribes its camera under /carla/hero/...; whether CARLA's own ROS 2 topics follow the role name has not been checked against a server yet. A camera in cameras is published under the topic it names, whatever the role name.
  • A camera in cameras publishes no sensor_msgs/CameraInfo.
  • Commands are read in the local frame frame_id names; nothing transforms a plan published in another frame (a Lanelet2 map, say).
  • control and steer_accel hand the acceleration to CARLA's Ackermann controller as given, as VisionPilot's relay does; the controller's own settings (AckermannControllerSettings) are CARLA's defaults.

docs.title: Scenario Editor
docs.text:
The Scenario Editor is a web UI for authoring scenarios declaratively and exporting them as self-contained wheelhouses. It runs as its own application:

uv run scenario-editor          # http://localhost:9100

It is deliberately separate from the Scenario Result Viewer (uv run viewer). Neither mounts the other, and running one does not start the other; integrating the two is a later phase.

docs.title: What it edits
docs.text:
The editor never edits Python. Its canonical representation is the Scenario IR -- a ScenarioDocument stored as YAML -- which the framework compiles into the existing runtime primitives:

ScenarioDocument -> ScenarioCompiler -> BaseAction / BaseCondition -> BaseScenario

There is no editor-only runtime. Every action a document names is built by autoware_carla_scenario.actions, every condition by autoware_carla_scenario.conditions, and every spawn constraint is evaluated by the same sweeper.constraints engine a --multirun sweep uses.

docs.title: Which map: the Map library
docs.text:
A scenario's map is named by a source URI pointing at a git repository, and the editor fetches and caches it. Map library in the header browses a repository -- HuggingFace, GitHub, your own -- and lists every map in it; the Scenario inspector shows, per scenario, whether the map is downloaded and whether its revision is pinned.

See HD Maps from a Git Repository. Two things are worth knowing here: a map Autoware's own setup already downloaded is used as it sits, and OpenDRIVE is not needed to author a scenario -- lanelets are.

docs.title: Where it happens: the places panel
docs.text:
One map carries every lanelet the scenario names -- each entity's spawn, the ego's goal, and the lanelet every condition watches. The canvas says what happens and in what order; it has no way to say where, and until this panel existed the answer was a scatter of ids across lane heads and condition cards that only meant something with the map open in another window.

It sits at the top of the right-hand rail, over the inspector:

+------------------------------------------+---------------------------+
| Arrangement (the timeline, full width)    | Places      < 1/133 >     |
| ACTOR | Init | 1  | 2  | 3  | 4  | 5      |   (o) NPC1 spawn BOUND    |
| Ego   |      | [] |    |    |    |        |   (o) Ego goal            |
| NPC1  |      | [] | [] |    |    |        |   (o) Ego spawn           |
| Env   |      |    | [] |    |    |        | [Ego spawn][Ego goal][..] |
| PASS  | ...                               +---------------------------+
| FAIL  | ...                               | Inspector                 |
+------------------------------------------+---------------------------+

Three things had to be true at once -- the map, the timeline and the inspector all on screen without scrolling -- and this is the arrangement that gets there without taking width from the thing that needs it. The timeline's axis is width: a card further right is later in the story, so narrowing it costs steps you can see. The map is roughly square and the inspector is a column, so both fit the rail; and "where" then sits directly over "what", which is what makes clicking a place and reading its object one movement of the eye.

The whole editor is one CSS grid (.ed-stage) for that reason. #editor-body stays the single htmx swap target and simply does not draw a box -- display: contents lifts the timeline and the inspector into that grid -- so the map can sit beside either of them while every edit still re-renders one element. Moving the panel is a change to one block of editor.css, not to a template.

Which glyph a place gets is the field's own declaration, not a guess from whatever holds it: FieldSpec.place is spawn, goal or watched, so the Set Goal action's lanelet draws as a destination exactly as the ego's own goal does. A primitive that registers a new lanelet field is drawn without the map learning anything about it.

Each place is a pin in its actor's track colour -- the same hue that actor's lane head and every condition naming it already wear -- with a glyph for what the place is: a target for a spawn, a flag for a goal, an eye for a lanelet something watches. The viewer has one highlight channel, so the outline says "this scenario touches here" and the pins say which of them is which.

Under the map the same places are chips, in document order. Clicking one opens the object that named it in the inspector and points the map at it; clicking a place on the map does the same, because the overview draws places the document already names and the only thing a click there can mean is "show me what named this". Nothing is edited here -- a lanelet is still set where it is written, in the picker its own field opens.

A label reads away from its dot, except on the right half of the map, where it reads back towards the middle: that edge is also where the viewer keeps its own zoom buttons, and a label running under them is a label nobody can read.

docs.title: An abstract scenario draws one bound pattern
docs.text:
A scenario whose lanelet is a constraint search does not name a place: it names a set, and the sweeper runs it once per member. Outlining all 133 matches draws the search, and none of those 133 runs looks like that picture. So one match is bound -- through the same swept_slot the exported config sweeps and the same constraint engine the sweep evaluates -- and the panel says which of how many is on screen. The arrows step through the runs a --multirun sweep would perform, one concrete scenario at a time.

Everything else keeps the id stored beside it, because that is exactly what a run that does not sweep uses: the sweeper enumerates a single target key, so at most one lanelet in a document is ever bound.

Binding means parsing the map on the server, which is measured in seconds, so it is a button (Bind a pattern) rather than something every page load pays for. Once the map is cached every later render binds without being asked, including the panel's own refresh after an edit.

docs.title: Where a pin goes
docs.text:
The labels are the server's -- rendered with the panel, beside the list that repeats them -- and only the coordinates are the viewer's. editor.js asks it through its public API: focusOn(id) centres the view on a primitive, so focusing one and reading getView() back reports that lanelet's centre in the map's own coordinates, and the view is then put back where it was. The alternative was projecting the .osm a second time in JavaScript, which is a second answer to "where is this" that can disagree with the drawing it is laid over. Each lanelet is measured once and kept on the frame, which is the frame reuseMap() parks across a re-render, so an edit re-places the pins without asking the map anything.

The panel frames itself on the places rather than on the whole city when the map loads, and a pan or zoom after that is the person's: a re-render carries it across, exactly as the picker's does. Tilted into the viewer's 3D view the pins hide themselves, because getView() then reports drawing coordinates and a point on a hill and the ground behind it are drawn in the same place.

This is a second parse of the same .osm while a picker is open, which is the cost the inspector's own map was removed to avoid. It is a different drawing rather than the same one twice: the picker answers "which lanelet is this field", and the overview answers "where is this scenario" -- a question nothing else on the page answers at all.

docs.title: The canvas
docs.text:
The main view is a swimlane DAG drawn as a DAW arrangement: one track per actor, with the horizontal axis reading as scenario progression, not time. Under the actors sits the Environment track, for actions no vehicle performs.

STEP >      | 1          | 2                 | 3
------------+------------+-------------------+------------------
Ego         | Drive      |                   |
------------+------------+-------------------+------------------
NPC1        | Follow     |                   | # Lane Change Left
            |            |                   |         ^
            |            |                   |   +-----+-----+
            |            |                   |   |    ALL    |
            |            |                   |  NPC1->Ego  NPC1->Ego
            |            |                   |  Distance   TTC
            |            |                   |  < 20 m     < 4 s
------------+------------+-------------------+------------------
Environment |            | Set Traffic Signal|
------------+------------+-------------------+------------------
PASS        | NPC1 enters the ego lane
FAIL        | Collision  | Timeout 30 s

docs.title: Which track an action belongs to
docs.text:
The action type decides, never the author. ActionSpec.scope is either actor or environment, and an environment action -- setting traffic lights, for instance -- is drawn in the Environment track whatever its actor field says. Nothing reads that field when such an action is built, so honouring it put the card in some vehicle's lane and claimed a relationship the run does not have. The editor no longer offers the field for one, refuses it on the way in, and drops a stale value on the next save; each track's + action menu offers only the actions that belong in it.

The Environment track is drawn even when it is empty, because it is where you go to add the first one. An action that merely has no actor yet is drawn there too: it is invalid, and a card nothing draws cannot be corrected.

The sequencer furniture is what makes the direction readable: track headers down the left, a numbered ruler across the top, a bar line before every slot and every other slot shaded. The ruler counts steps and not seconds, which is the whole reason it is a step ruler -- see the first rule below.

docs.title: What a step is
docs.text:
Nothing in Python has a "step". The runtime arms every action from the first tick and ticks them all every frame:

for action in scenario._pre_tick_actions:
    action.tick(world, elapsed)
